headline:
Who will be there
between visits?
support: A practical question for Westlake Village families

GBP.title: Westlake Village: planning support between hospice visits
GBP.caption:
For a Westlake Village family considering hospice at home, one practical question matters: who will be there between visits?

Hospice visits follow an individualized care plan. Having clinical support available by phone 24/7 is not the same as continuous bedside nursing or a live-in caregiver.

Our Journal guide offers questions about daily help, family schedules, care-team contacts and what to do when needs change. At Eternal Life Hospice, that conversation begins with listening to the person’s wishes and the household’s needs.

Read the guide to prepare for your family’s care conversation.

Facebook.title: A care plan also needs a plan between visits
Facebook.caption:
A care plan also needs a plan for the hours between visits.

If your family is considering hospice at home, it helps to talk through the ordinary parts of the day: who can be present, who can help with daily needs and whom to call when something changes.

Hospice visits follow an individualized plan. Clinical guidance available by phone 24/7 does not mean a nurse stays at the bedside around the clock or that hospice provides a live-in caregiver.

Our new guide is written for Westlake Village families planning those conversations. You do not have to have every answer before you ask for help.

Read the guide: {url}

#WestlakeVillage #FamilyCaregiving #HospiceCare

LinkedIn.title: Make the hours between hospice visits part of the conversation
LinkedIn.caption:
The hours between hospice visits belong in the care-planning conversation.

For families and referral partners, understanding the visit plan is only part of preparing for hospice at home. Daily support, household availability and an agreed contact for changes in needs deserve equal clarity.

An individualized hospice plan does not establish continuous bedside staffing. Clinical support available by phone 24/7 is distinct from live-in caregiving or around-the-clock nursing in the home.

At Eternal Life Hospice, the first conversation starts with the person’s wishes and the household’s practical needs. Clear expectations can help families ask more useful questions and identify what still needs to be arranged.

Our Westlake Village Journal guide provides a starting point for that discussion.

Read the guide: {url}

#HospiceCare #CareCoordination #WestlakeVillage

headline:
Before you sign,
ask your questions.

GBP.title: The hospice election statement: a conversation, not a test
GBP.caption:
Hospice paperwork should leave room for questions.

The hospice election statement records important choices about care and coverage. Before signing, ask the team to explain what the election means, which services relate to the terminal illness and what costs or services may fall outside the benefit.

Our Journal article offers a plain-language starting point for that conversation. An election statement, an advance directive and decision-maker documents serve different purposes; your care team can help clarify the distinctions.

Read the guide and bring your questions to the team.

headline:
Comfort starts
with permission.
support: Listening first. Respecting each person’s choice.

GBP.title: Personalized comfort begins with a choice
GBP.caption:
Some people welcome gentle sound. Others prefer silence. Personalized comfort begins by asking—not assuming.

At Eternal Life Hospice, conversations about comfort start with the person’s wishes, privacy and daily routines. Optional sound bathing may offer a setting for relaxation and feeling more settled; it is not a medical treatment and does not replace licensed care. Choosing quiet deserves the same respect.

Our Journal article explores consent, optional nonclinical support and how a person’s preferences guide the conversation.

Read “Personalized Comfort Starts With Permission.”

Facebook.title: Comfort starts with permission
Facebook.caption:
Sometimes the most thoughtful question is, “Would you like this—or would you prefer quiet?”

A familiar routine, gentle sound or a calm moment can mean different things to different people. Comfort is personal, and a person’s choice can change from day to day.

At Eternal Life Hospice, optional sound bathing is offered as a preference-led comfort experience—a space for relaxation and feeling more grounded, not a medical treatment. Some people may welcome it. Others may choose silence. Both choices deserve respect.

These offerings do not replace symptom assessment, medications or licensed care. Sound bathing is not covered by Medicare or Medi-Cal; Eternal provides it at no additional expense to families, subject to availability and fit.

Read how permission shapes personalized comfort: {url}

#PersonCenteredCare #HospiceComfort #EternalLifeHospice

LinkedIn.title: Person-centered comfort begins with permission
LinkedIn.caption:
A comfort offering is only person-centered when declining it is a genuine option.

Personalization begins with listening to wishes, routines and privacy preferences—not with assuming that the same experience will feel comforting to everyone.

At Eternal Life Hospice, optional sound bathing is framed as a preference-led opportunity for relaxation and feeling more settled. It is not offered to diagnose, treat or cure, and it does not replace symptom assessment, medications or licensed care.

A person may welcome gentle sound, prefer a familiar routine or choose quiet. Consent can change, and the plan should respect that.

Sound bathing is not covered by Medicare or Medi-Cal. Eternal provides it at no additional expense to families, subject to availability and fit.

Our latest Journal article explores these boundaries and the role of optional nonclinical support.

Read the article: {url}

#PersonCenteredCare #HospiceCare #PatientChoice

headline:
A thoughtful
care handoff.
support: Planning a thoughtful care handoff in Calabasas

GBP.title: Calabasas: planning a thoughtful care handoff
GBP.caption:
A move into assisted living involves more than transferring a medication list.

For Calabasas families considering hospice during a transition, it helps to share familiar routines, communication preferences, privacy boundaries and the names of the people who should receive updates.

Clarify responsibilities between the residence and hospice team, including daily assistance, medication coordination and after-hours contacts. Hospice visits do not replace the facility’s staffing or provide continuous bedside nursing.

Our Journal checklist offers questions to help families plan a thoughtful handoff. Read the guide.

headline:
Keep what
feels familiar.
support: Small traditions. Room for rest. A person’s choice.

GBP.title: Keeping familiar traditions during hospice care
GBP.caption:
A tradition can become smaller and still feel meaningful.

A familiar photograph, favorite music or a short visit may be enough to keep a sense of connection. During hospice care, the person’s energy, comfort and wishes can guide what the day looks like—including choosing rest or quiet instead.

At Eternal Life Hospice, planning begins with listening. Our Journal article explores ways families can keep ordinary seasonal traditions flexible, without making participation an expectation.

Read “Keeping Ordinary Traditions During Hospice Care.”

Facebook.title: A smaller tradition can still feel like yours
Facebook.caption:
A smaller tradition can still feel like yours.

A favorite photograph. Familiar music. A short visit with someone who understands when it is time to rest.

During hospice care, a meaningful day does not have to look the way it used to. Traditions can change with a person’s energy and wishes, without becoming another thing the family feels it must get right.

Ask what feels welcome today. Make room for a different answer tomorrow. Choosing quiet or sitting something out is a choice worth honoring, too.

Our latest Journal article shares a thoughtful approach to keeping ordinary traditions familiar and manageable.

Read the article: {url}

#FamilyConnection #HospiceCare #CareThatHonorsLife

LinkedIn.title: Familiar routines belong in person-centered care
LinkedIn.caption:
Person-centered care makes room for ordinary traditions—and the choice to change them.

Seasonal routines can carry meaning for a person receiving hospice care. A familiar photograph, a brief visit or favorite music may offer connection without asking the person to participate beyond what feels welcome.

The care-planning question is not how to reproduce a perfect occasion. It is what the person wants today, what feels tiring and what can be simplified or left out.

At Eternal Life Hospice, listening to those preferences helps keep the conversation grounded in the individual. Privacy, energy and the option to decline remain important, even when a family’s intentions are loving.

Our Journal article offers families and care partners a starting point for that conversation.

Read the article: {url}

#PersonCenteredCare #FamilyCaregiving #HospiceCare
